files.rationale: Most claim units are carried, mostly in a condensed or changed form, by the promoted host-invocation-routing documents (vision, kernel, host use cases, provider routing, contracts, release boundaries); a minority (canonical-name rule, contract versioning, lifecycle state chain, idempotency key rule, physical placement and open questions) are absent and recorded as blocking.

claims.rationale: The document title is replaced by the area portal title "Host Invocation"; the old combined name "Host Invocation And Provider Routing Architecture" appears in no target heading.

Targets carry only a header block (Design status: Draft, Source type: Promoted from ...); the source status "vision/architecture advisory, not a locked platform law and not an implementation plan", the 2026-09-10 date and the link to the design review it was revised against are not stated.

The vision paragraph states the same host-independent and provider-independent invocation foundation, but it does not call it the permanent "kernel contract" and the cross-links to the companion documents are replaced by the promoted architecture set.
The portal states the old documents remain legacy-current sources until redirected or drained; the source heading is its own legacy-promotion note, reworded as "Migration Notes".

README Migration Notes says the old documents stay legacy/current until redirected; it does not repeat the per-file split list (vision, kernel, host use cases, provider routing, contracts), which survives only as the Read First table links.
The name and the two-step idea (host admits/normalizes, router selects) live in the vision; the heading "Architecture Name" itself is gone.

The source records a naming decision: Component Router rejected because not every component is a dispatchable provider, Command Router rejected because commands are only a CLI projection of semantic operations. No target states these rejected names or reasons; only the name "Operation Provider Router" appears in vision.
searched: Operation Provider Router (vision.md only, no rejected-name rationale)

claims.rationale: The vision paragraph states the same split: a host admits and normalizes caller context, the Operation Provider Router selects an implementation.
The problem framing is carried by the vision section; heading "Problem And Scope" is not present as such (vision has "Non-Scope").

The vision says the three-axis model avoids a special-path matrix per host/plugin/legacy; the source reasons about differing parsing, auth context, streaming and response projection and names the Cartesian product, which the vision omits.
Heading of the canonical-names table, whose entries are spread over operation-provider, operation-request-outcome, operation-catalog, provider-routing, invocation-kernel and command-route-descriptor.
The rule "one name per concept; no alias appears anywhere in this document or its two companions" is not stated in any target.

Every name in the table is defined across targets: OperationProvider, ProviderDescriptor, InvocationControl, EventSink, ConfigPort in operation-provider.md; HostInvocation, OperationRequest, ContractRef, ProviderOutcome, ProviderError in operation-request-outcome.md; OperationId, OperationDescriptor, OperationCatalog in operation-catalog.md; Router and RegistrySnapshot in provider-routing.md; InvocationService in invocation-kernel.md; CommandRouteDescriptor in command-route-descriptor.md. Descriptions are condensed and section references dropped.
Heading for the peer host use cases section, carried by the host-use-cases architecture document.
Target states that cli-host-use-case, remote-host-use-case and chat-host-use-case are peers and none wraps, shells out to, or calls through another.

Spec keeps the text pipeline (HostInvocation+OperationRequest -> InvocationService -> Router.select -> grant -> invoke -> ProviderOutcome -> presenter); the host-adapter topology, CommandRouteDescriptor lookup with the dashed legacy exec arrow, and the provider kinds list of the diagram are not carried.
Target states LegacyCliPassthroughProvider is CLI-only and bypasses the kernel, and spec section 5 forbids routing legacy through InvocationService; same meaning as the dashed-arrow note.

Target table keeps owns/never-does per host but omits verb to OperationId mapping and CommandRouteDescriptor lookup for CLI, and for remote omits not treating HTTP as an internal API and not spawning bin/fgos.mjs; chat never-does is shortened.
Alignment table says the remote peer is the project-local gateway in R3 but drops "current herdr, same release" and the pointer to the future shared gateway constraint.

Kernel claim states one semantic input/output boundary and that InvocationService owns the pipeline; the explicit deliberate-reuse rule (all projectors build the same HostInvocation/OperationRequest, presenters stay separate) and "peer status does not require one OS process, separate binaries compose the same host-runtime crate" are not stated.

Target keeps bypass of the kernel, Node-owned arg parsing and no double fgos.v1 wrapping; it does not state that the lane lives in the CLI adapter, argv preserved with inherited stdin/cwd/env, signal forwarding, or one invocation record.
Heading for core contracts; the contracts index carries the set of contract documents.

Pure cross-reference sentence: "The name table (§3) says what each type is; this adds the rules it has no room for." It points at section numbers of a document that has been split into per-contract targets.

Target keeps the OperationId shape and that host spellings are projections; it drops component-owns-authority, singular object-type, the small verb set, the examples (work.item.submit, distribution.build.show), REST plural URL mapping, and not suffixing compatible field additions.
Target states host kind is an open string; the literal examples cli/remote/chat and "not a closed enum" wording are condensed.
Target says OperationRequest carries OperationId, ContractRef and typed semantic input; the concrete Box<dyn Any + Send> shape and that built-ins downcast directly are not stated.

Kernel bullets state built-ins use typed Rust inputs and never decode EncodedMessage, and raw CLI OsString is never a semantic request; component-protocol limits EncodedMessage to the external boundary.

Target says ProviderOutcome is not a CLI envelope, HTTP response, MCP result or chat text; it omits that the presenter owns public projection and that diagnostics travel via the trace/evidence sink rather than compatibility stdout/stderr.

Target keeps open-string mechanism, LegacySemanticProvider-style legacy-node and ConfigPort; it omits the lifecycle values singleton|per-invocation|pooled, the closed list of mechanism strings, and the note that the CLI exec lane is not a provider.

Target keeps catalog authored by owning components, not inferred from CLI registry or manifests, and the descriptor field list; it omits the effect and idempotency value sets, CLI registry authority for help/grammar, build_snapshot, kernel not depending on provider crates, and the R1 no-linker/cache/manifest-scan rule.

Contract versioning rules are absent: request/outcome contracts version independently, linking picks one exact version pair from the host/provider range intersection with no best-effort coercion, incompatible change means a new variant or major version, explicit registered upgrade/downgrade transforms recorded in diagnostics, router never reshapes payloads.
Heading for router and InvocationService pipeline, carried by the provider-routing architecture claim.

Target says the Router is a pure selection function and InvocationService owns everything not selection; the explicit list no I/O, no async, no invocation, no failure normalization, no reporting is not stated.
Target lists the same router inputs (OperationId, contract versions, host kind, mode, project policy, RegistrySnapshot); the result type Result<ProviderDescriptor, SelectionRefused> is not stated.

Target keeps fail-closed duplicates unless an explicit replacement names both providers; it omits that the router never parses CLI/HTTP input, admits, grants, holds domain policy, lets a provider recursively spawn fgos, or renders a response.
Kernel states InvocationService owns the pipeline stages; the sentence that it is the only thing that invokes a provider is not stated.
Kernel claim lists the same pipeline stages in order: admission, router call, selected-provider grant, invocation, failure normalization, lifecycle recording.

Target keeps closed failure families with presenter mapping after outcome and exactly one terminal record; it omits invoke running with deadline/cancellation/trace context, normalization leaving semantic errors unchanged, and reporting the serving provider and registry fingerprint.

Target keeps no priority/registration-order/last-writer-wins and named replacement; it omits that a binding names one provider, that replacement also names an authorizing policy, and the RegistrySnapshot immutability rules (assembled once in R1, atomic publish between invocations from R2).

Target says OperationProvider exposes descriptor() and asynchronous invoke(...); the Rust trait signature (Send+Sync, HostInvocation, OperationRequest, InvocationControl, EventSink, boxed future of Result<ProviderOutcome, ProviderError>) is not given.
Heading for authority; the target section "Authority" carries the two-stage model.

Manifest rules keep reserved core namespaces, vendor-scoped operations, fail-closed unknown/ambiguous claims and config never replacing a built-in; missing are the explicit capability grants for .fgos writes, Git mutation and process/network/secret access, and the R1-R2 rollback-through-fgctl-with-both-providers-shipped statement (only partly in release-boundaries and vision).
Provider routing states provider manifests request capabilities and never grant authority.

Target lists caller admission before routing and selected-provider grant after routing; the admission inputs (principal, operation, project policy, requested context, host surface) and that grant intersects the admitted action with the operation capability policy and provider requested capabilities are not stated.

Target states the provider gets only the least-privilege grant through InvocationControl; "identically for every host" and the reason a single pre-selection gate cannot evaluate provider identity, trust or capability request are not stated.

README says provider selection never transfers ownership of a state write and Work Lifecycle, Dispatch and Run Result Evaluation authority is not taken; it omits that a replacement returns a result or proof, the per-owner rules (Run Result Evaluation computes confidence without choosing status; Dispatch cannot invent its operation) and that a manifest claim never grants .fgos, Git, process, network or secret access.
Heading for failure, cancellation, lifecycle and human input; carried by the failure-families, lifecycle and human-input sections of the request/outcome contract.
Target states the closed failure families as common across invocation mechanisms.
Target lists all fourteen closed failure families of the source list.

Kernel keeps presenter mapping after the provider outcome; component-protocol keeps completion-unknown after crash unless idempotency permits retry and operation-provider keeps the async port; missing are preserved invocation/provider IDs for correlation, no crash-as-semantic-failure or success inferred from partial output, remote disconnect cancelling through the same context as CLI interrupt, and the async-from-v1 rationale.

The lifecycle state chain received -> admitted|admission-refused -> selected|selection-refused -> granted|grant-refused -> dispatched -> succeeded|semantic-failed|cancelled|deadline-exceeded|provider-failed|completion-unknown is not in any target; only dispatched, completion-unknown and one terminal record are named.

Target states exactly one terminal record, dispatched as the point where transport loss becomes completion-unknown, and late responses as diagnostics; the record field list (invocation/parent-correlation ID, contract versions, registry fingerprint, provider ID, host kind, timing, terminal family, evidence references, never secrets) is not stated.

Idempotency-key rule is absent: the key lives in the owning operation contract and is stable across an authorized retry, the router never invents one, and read-only does not imply retry-safe with external effects (catalog idempotency decides). Targets only list idempotency as a descriptor field and tie crash retry to the idempotency contract.
Target states providers never block waiting for a person and return a parked outcome that the host or Work Lifecycle re-invokes later.
Heading of the Physical Placement section whose content (public name, fgctl separation, naming conventions, crate layout, R1 crate count) is not carried by any target.

Public command name stays fgos because runtime identity is the release digest; fgctl is a separate bootstrap binary, not a renamed fgos; crates kebab-case with fgos- prefix, modules snake_case. Targets only say bin/fgos.mjs is not renamed.

The target directory/crate layout tree (apps/fgos, apps/gateway, packages/host-runtime/rust modules, distribution, component-protocol) is not stated as intended layout in any target; only individual source paths appear as evidence links.

Placement rules are absent: R1 is three crates (fgos, fgos-host-runtime, fgos-distribution), legacy exec lane is a module in apps/fgos not a crate, component-protocol waits for R2, extract crates only under real pressure, neither app owns provider selection, no host use case imports another, a component is not created for one proof verb (only the gate-policy remark survives in roadmap).

README states the host consumes the runtime selected by Packaging-Distribution and does not own fgctl, acquisition, activation, upgrade, repair or rollback; the onboarding vocabulary (fgos init adopts a workspace, fgos doctor --fix performs repairs, no separate setup verb) is not stated in any target of this area.
Heading for release boundaries; target section "Release Boundaries" carries the R1/R2/R3 table.

Target keeps R1/R2/R3 required slices and not-gates but changed: R2 derived cache is in-memory only (no by-fingerprint load, no explicit test/dev roots), and R3 is narrowed to GET /v1/runtime with different non-gates; the Project Runtime Adapter statement for a future shared gateway and the per-operation Node semantic bridge are not stated.

Chat as a future peer not gating R1/R2 is carried in README and spec; the "Ship the Rust host" definition appears only as "reproducible install/activation/rollback proof", without the target matrix, external-project install test, named rollback channel or the repo-tests-alone-is-a-candidate statement.
Spec has an Unknowns section listing different closed/open items; the source heading Open Questions is replaced by it.

Five open questions: which capabilities ship as packaged extensions vs core; exact OperationIds and projections for first native operations; which extension points are public in the first ecosystem release; whether a later protocol version adds a local socket transport; integrity/signature policy separating local dev plugins from distributable ones. Only the OperationId question has a counterpart (spec unknowns); marketplace/signatures appear only as out of R2 scope.

README says install, activation, upgrade and rollback belong to Packaging-Distribution; the source also states target matrix, install/upgrade mechanism and R1 definition are owned by packaging and links the Runtime Identity And Activation document, which this README does not name.
Heading for related documents; README section "Related Files" carries the link table.

README related table links the promoted equivalents (external-provider-protocol, legacy-cli-transition, node-to-rust-migration, packaging README, component boundary); the links to the Rust host implementation plan and the component-boundary advisory are not carried.
